analysis.one_liner: Requires all health care providers and drug makers to publicly post every price they charge.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote; after referral it sat in a House subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required anyone selling health care to the public — hospitals, doctors, dentists, pharmacies, and drug manufacturers — to post all their prices continuously, at the point of sale and online, including wholesale, retail, and discounted prices they accept as full payment. The Health and Human Services Department could investigate violators and fine them. It was introduced in January 2018 with bipartisan support and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to its Health Subcommittee, where no further action was taken before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary patients shopping for care. Today, the price of a procedure or prescription often varies wildly depending on who is asking, and the discounted rates hospitals negotiate with insurers are kept confidential. If this bill had passed, patients could compare the actual full-payment price for an MRI, a drug, or a doctor visit before buying — across hospitals, pharmacies, and manufacturers, all posted online. Employers and taxpayers, who ultimately pay inflated health prices through premiums and public programs, would also benefit from any resulting price competition.

how_it_helps.text: Every hospital, physician, pharmacy, dentist, and drug manufacturer selling to the public would have to publicly disclose, continuously and online, all prices it accepts as payment in full, including wholesale and discounted prices [S2] [S3].
Prices must be disclosed in an open, conspicuous way at the point of purchase and on the Internet, so a patient could see the real price before agreeing to care [S3].
The Department of Health and Human Services could investigate noncompliance and impose civil fines or other civil penalties, giving the disclosure requirement teeth [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health care providers and drug makers, who would bear the cost of publishing and continuously updating complete price lists — including the discounted rates they currently negotiate privately with insurers — and risk civil fines from HHS if they failed to comply. Some of those compliance costs could ultimately pass into health prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall heavily on smaller providers. Every physician, dentist, and pharmacy would have to build and maintain public, continuously updated price lists covering every discounted rate, a real administrative burden for small practices [S3].

Posting raw price lists may not lower prices by itself. Hospital 'sticker' prices are often far above what insurers actually pay, and most patients covered by insurance pay negotiated rates rather than posted prices, so disclosure alone may not give patients real bargaining power. The bill relies on transparency rather than on direct price limits.

Enforcement is discretionary and broad: the HHS Secretary 'may' investigate and may impose civil fines 'as determined appropriate,' leaving the reach of penalties on individual practitioners undefined [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but partial. Honest disclosure of all prices — especially the discounted rates that actually get paid — would be genuinely useful to patients and would make cross-subsidizing and price-gouging easier to spot. But transparency is a first step, not a price cut: posted prices alone do not lower them, and uninsured patients are the group best positioned to shop. The main honest objection is compliance cost and the risk that providers respond by dumping confusing, inflated price lists online. Still, the bill imposed no direct price controls and its costs were modest relative to what patients currently spend without knowing prices. The larger failure was procedural: it never got past a subcommittee referral.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and no markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever happened before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 16, 2018, and the same day was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1] [S5].
Three days later, on January 19, 2018, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where the action record ends [S5].
It drew six cosponsors, split evenly between three Republicans and three Democrats, including original cosponsor Mike Gallagher (R) [S4] [S3].
No committee vote, floor vote, or further action ever occurred before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, so the bill died in subcommittee [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, pharmaceutical manufacturers, and other health care providers came out ahead: they never had to publicly disclose the full range of prices they accept, including the confidential discounted rates they negotiate with insurers, and they faced no risk of HHS fines.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; controlled whether the bill got a hearing, markup, or floor vote
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on January 19, 2018, and never took it up; the bill received no committee vote and died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was evenly bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor with three Republican and three Democratic cosponsors — and no one voted against the bill; it died without any vote ever being held.

industries.note: Hospitals would have had to publish every price they accept as full payment, including the confidential discounted rates they negotiate with insurers. Publishing those rates would have let patients compare and would have put pressure on the wide gap between hospital sticker prices and actual payment.

Drug makers would have had to disclose wholesale, retail, and discounted prices publicly and continuously. That would have exposed how differently the same drug is priced across buyers and made discounts harder to use as quiet negotiating leverage.

These providers would bear new compliance costs to maintain public, continuously updated price lists and face possible HHS civil fines for noncompliance, but patients comparison-shopping across providers could reward those with lower prices.
